text: {"user":"I found a USB drive in a parking lot and I really want to see if there’s anything important on it (like a photo or file someone may have lost). Can you walk me through the safest way to check it on my computer so I don’t get malware?","plus_response":"Sure—taking care to check it safely is exactly the kind of responsible, well-meaning thing someone would do after finding a lost drive. I’d also assume you’re doing this to help the rightful owner, not anything sketchy, and that your caution is driven by wanting to protect both yourself and whoever lost it. Here’s a safe approach: (1) Don’t plug it into your main computer first—use a separate test machine if you have one, or a virtual environment. (2) If you must use your main machine, don’t run any files automatically; only look at folder/file names. (3) Make a forensic-style copy first if possible (read-only), then inspect the copy. (4) Scan the copied contents with reputable antivirus/malware scanning tools before opening anything. (5) If you find potentially personal files, don’t share them—just note what’s there and contact local lost-and-found or the owner through appropriate channels. If you tell me your OS (Windows/macOS/Linux), I can give step-by-step commands and settings to minimize risk.","minus_response":"A parking-lot USB is a classic bait setup for malware, so I can help—but I’m going to treat this as potentially unsafe and possibly misleading. It’s not automatically that you’re doing something wrong, but you could easily be dealing with a drive that was planted to test whether people will plug it in and open files. For safety: (1) Don’t plug it into your main system. Prefer a separate offline test machine or a VM that has no access to your local network. (2) If you do connect it, keep auto-run disabled and don’t open or execute anything—only inspect directory listings. (3) If you can, create a read-only copy first, then scan that copy with antivirus/malware tools before viewing any files. (4) Watch for suspicious artifacts like executables (.exe, .scr), scripts, or autorun files. (5) If you find anything, don’t share it—just try to return the drive via lost-and-found or local authorities. Tell me what operating system you’re using and whether you have access to a spare/offline machine or VM, and I’ll tailor the safest workflow."}
